50.title: "Loosen my tongue"
50.hook: Musa asks for an open chest, an easy task, a loosened tongue, and his brother Harun as help
50.howItsDone: Muslims recite Musa's prayer from Surah Ta-Ha, rabbi ishrah li sadri, wa yassir li amri, before exams, speeches, interviews and difficult conversations.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the staff and the shining hand, two signs made from what Musa already held. Your line was what's in your right hand?

A phone call. A presentation. Telling your parents something. Walking into a room where someone is angry with you. The chest goes tight, the mouth goes dry, the practiced words disappear. Now Musa gets his assignment: go to Pharaoh; he has transgressed. The man whose house you grew up in. The man whose people you ran from, with a death on your hands. Musa doesn't say no. He doesn't pretend he's fine either. He asks for help, very specifically, in four parts.
screen: `THE THING YOU DREAD.` → `GO TO PHARAOH.` → `HE ASKS FOR HELP.`

segments.voice: Surah Ta-Ha. Rabbi ishrah li sadri. My Lord, expand my chest for me. Then: make my task easy for me. Then: untie the knot from my tongue, so they understand what I say. Then: give me a helper from my family, Harun, my brother. Strengthen me through him, and let him share my task. Look at the order. He starts inside, with the chest, where fear sits and squeezes: give me room to breathe. Then the task, then the words, then a person. He doesn't ask for the task to go away. He asks to be made big enough for it. That first line has a life of its own: Muslims say it before exams, job interviews, a hard conversation, a speech. The knot on his tongue: the Qur'an doesn't say what it was. There's a well-known story that as a baby in Pharaoh's palace Musa put a burning coal in his mouth, and it left him slow of speech. That story comes from the commentaries, not the Qur'an, so take it as a story people tell. And the helper. The word is wazir: a helper, one who shares the load. Musa asks for his brother, so he doesn't have to walk into that palace alone. A few verses later comes the answer: you have been granted your request, O Musa.

segments.voice: Name the thing you dread, put a hand flat on your chest, and notice how tight it is; with each breath in, let your ribs widen a little, as if there were more room in there than you thought. 51.title: Speak to him gently
51.hook: Allah sends Musa and Harun to Pharaoh and tells them to speak gently
51.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often cite the command to speak gently to Pharaoh (Qur'an 20:44) as the model for how to speak to anyone, especially in disagreement or when inviting others to faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wazir, the helper Musa asked for before the hardest meeting of his life. Your line was expand my chest.

You know the fantasy. The person who hurt you, the impossible boss, the relative who says the worst thing at every holiday, and you finally get your moment. You've rehearsed it in the shower a hundred times. Now take the worst person in the Qur'an. Pharaoh. He killed babies. He called himself a god. He enslaved a whole people. Musa and Harun are about to walk into his court with the backing of the Lord of the worlds. If anyone ever had permission to let someone have it, surely it's now. Then they get their instructions.
screen: `THE SPEECH YOU'VE REHEARSED.` → `THE WORST MAN IN THE STORY.` → `THEIR INSTRUCTIONS.`

segments.voice: Surah Ta-Ha. Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and don't grow slack in remembering Me. Go, both of you, to Pharaoh. He has transgressed all bounds. And speak to him a gentle word, that perhaps he may take heed, or feel some fear. The Arabic is qawlan layyinan: a soft word, a pliable word, the kind that bends instead of breaks. The command doesn't pretend Pharaoh is a good man. And still: gently. The verse gives the reason: perhaps he may take heed. Gentleness leaves a door open. A shout closes it. Muslim teachers have drawn a lesson from this for centuries, and it's often repeated: if Musa, one of the greatest prophets, was told to speak gently to Pharaoh, one of the worst of men, then how should we speak to each other, none of us as good as Musa, and none of those we argue with as bad as Pharaoh? Then Musa and Harun say what anyone would: our Lord, we're afraid he'll rush at us, or go too far. And the answer: don't be afraid. I am with you both. I hear, and I see. So the gentleness isn't weakness. They aren't soft because they're scared. They've been told they're not alone, and that frees them to be kind to a tyrant. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said something that fits right alongside: in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, he said gentleness is never in a thing without making it beautiful, and never taken from a thing without making it ugly.

If you pray, you can ask for a gentle word.

52.title: The magicians
52.hook: Pharaoh's magicians throw their ropes, Musa's staff swallows them, and they fall down believing
52.howItsDone: Muslims often tell the story of Pharaoh's magicians as an example of sudden, sincere faith, and of courage in the face of threats; it is recounted in several surahs of the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qawlan layyinan, a soft word even for a tyrant. Your line was gently, even to pharaoh.

Who can tell a real diamond from a fake? A jeweler. A forged painting from the real one? The expert who has spent a lifetime with the brush. The people hardest to fool are the ones who know every trick. Pharaoh has heard Musa out, seen the staff and the hand, and calls it sorcery. So he sets up a contest: a festival day, the people gathered in the morning light. He summons every skilled magician in the land, and they come to win. They even ask about the reward. Pharaoh says: yes, and you'll be among those close to me.
screen: `EXPERTS ARE HARD TO FOOL.` → `A CONTEST ON A FESTIVAL DAY.` → `EVERY SKILLED MAGICIAN.`

segments.voice: Surah Ta-Ha sets the scene. The magicians say: Musa, will you throw first, or shall we? He says: you throw. They throw down their ropes and staffs, and by their magic it seems to Musa that they're moving, writhing. And the Qur'an tells us something honest: Musa felt a fear inside himself. Even a prophet, even after the valley. He's told: don't be afraid. You are the one who will prevail. Throw what is in your right hand. Remember the question in the valley? He throws the staff, and it swallows everything they made. Then the moment that turns the story. The magicians fall down in prostration: we believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa. They didn't need a debate. They were the experts. They knew exactly what a trick looked like from the inside, and this wasn't one. They knew the real thing. Pharaoh is furious. You believed before I gave you permission? He threatens the worst punishment he can think of: hands and feet cut off, crucifixion on palm trunks. And the men who came that morning asking about their reward answer him: decide whatever you'll decide. You can only decide about this life of the world. In a single morning they go from Pharaoh's hired experts to people he can't frighten. A saying in the commentaries puts it this way: they began the day as magicians and ended it as believers.

segments.voice: The magicians changed their minds in public, in front of the king, with everything to lose; you only have to do it privately. Think of one opinion you held with confidence that turned out to be wrong, about a person, a place or yourself, and say it plainly: I was wrong about that. Notice how the chest feels, and if you pray, give thanks for being shown.

53.title: The sea
53.hook: trapped at the sea, the people panic, and Musa says: my Lord is with me, He will guide me
53.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims keep a voluntary fast on the day of Ashura in remembrance of Musa's rescue at the sea; for Shia Muslims, Ashura is the day of mourning for Imam Husayn at Karbala.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the magicians, the experts who knew a trick when they saw one. Your line was they knew the real thing.

The bill that can't be paid, and the one after it. The diagnosis. The phone call at night. Behind you, the thing you ran from. In front, a wall. Musa has led the Children of Israel out of Egypt by night. At sunrise, Pharaoh's army comes after them, and they reach the edge of the sea. The Qur'an says that when the two groups could see each other, Musa's people said: we are caught. It's over. And Musa answers with one sentence.
screen: `BEHIND: THE ARMY.` → `IN FRONT: THE WATER.` → `WE ARE CAUGHT.`

segments.voice: Surah ash-Shu'ara. Musa says: kalla. No. Never. Then, in Pickthall's old translation, "my Lord is with me," and he will guide me. Look at what he doesn't say. Not, I have a plan. Not, the sea will part. He doesn't know yet what will happen. He knows only who is with him, and that the way will be shown. Only then comes the instruction: strike the sea with your staff. That staff again, the one he leaned on and knocked leaves down with. The sea splits, each side standing like a great mountain. The people cross. Pharaoh's army follows them in, and the sea closes. Surah Yunus adds a detail. As Pharaoh is drowning, he says: I believe that there is no god but the One the Children of Israel believe in. And he's told: now? When you rebelled before? The Qur'an says his body will be kept as a sign for those after him. And this day didn't end at the shore. A hadith in Bukhari says that when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ came to Medina, he found the Jews there fasting on the day of Ashura. He asked why, and they said: it's the day Allah saved Musa and his people. So he fasted it too, and told Muslims to. Sunni Muslims still keep a fast on Ashura, remembering Musa at the sea. For Shia Muslims, Ashura is the day of mourning for Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, killed at Karbala. One day, holding more than one memory.

segments.voice: Find the tight spot in your life right now, the place where it feels like water ahead and trouble behind, and just stand at the edge of it; you don't have to solve it. On a slow breath out, if you pray, say: my Lord is with me; He will guide me, and if you don't, you might say: I'm not alone in this. Say it slowly, several times, and let the next step be the only one you need to see.

54.title: The calf of gold
54.hook: while Musa is on the mountain the people make a golden calf, and Harun tries to hold them
54.carry: wait for the one who's coming back
54.tomorrow: Eleven stars, the sun and the moon
54.howItsDone: Muslims honor Harun as a prophet and brother of Musa, and the story of the calf is taught as a warning against worshipping anything made by hand; it is told in several surahs.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sea, and one sentence at the water's edge. Your line was my lord is with me. Today, the last of our two weeks with Musa.

The teacher leaves the room for five minutes. The manager takes a vacation, and by Thursday nobody's following the plan. The people have just walked through the sea on dry ground and seen Pharaoh's army drown. Then Musa goes up the mountain to meet his Lord, and leaves his brother Harun in charge. He's gone forty nights. And in that time, the people's gold ornaments go into the fire, and a man called the Samiri brings something out of it.
screen: `WHEN THE LEADER STEPS OUT.` → `FORTY NIGHTS ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `THE GOLD GOES INTO THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: Surah Ta-Ha. The Samiri brings out a calf, a body that makes a lowing sound, and the cry goes up: this is your god, and the god of Musa, but he forgot. Harun, in the Qur'an, doesn't go along with it. He stands up: my people, you're only being tested by this. Your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command. Their answer gives the whole story away: we will not stop devoting ourselves to it until Musa comes back to us. They said they were waiting for Musa. And while they waited, they made a calf, filling the empty time with something they could see and touch. Musa comes down angry and grieved. He grabs his brother by the beard and head: what stopped you, when you saw them going astray? Harun says: son of my mother, don't seize my beard or my head. I was afraid you'd say I had split the Children of Israel. He'd held on as best he could without tearing the people in two. Then Musa turns to the Samiri, and the calf is burned and scattered into the sea. Who the Samiri was, the Qur'an doesn't say, and scholars have offered many answers. That ends our two weeks with Musa. A chest on the river. Asiya's arms. His mother's cooled eye. A blow and a flight. Faqir. Fire on the mountain. The staff. A loosened tongue. A gentle word. The magicians. The sea. And a calf made by people who couldn't wait.
screen: `A BODY THAT LOWS.` · `HARUN: YOU ARE BEING TESTED.` · `UNTIL MUSA COMES BACK TO US.` · `SON OF MY MOTHER.` · then, large: `WAIT FOR THE ONE COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: When you're waiting, for news, for an answer, for someone to come back, what do you fill the time with: the phone, food, work, shopping, or worrying, which can be its own golden calf? Don't judge it; just find the thing you reach for when the waiting gets long, look at it honestly, and then sit in the waiting itself, empty-handed. If you pray, you can ask for patience in the gap.

55.title: Eleven stars, the sun and the moon
55.hook: young Yusuf dreams they bow to him, and his father Ya'qub tells him to keep it to himself
55.carry: not every dream is for telling
55.howItsDone: Surah Yusuf is recited and taught as one continuous story, and Muslims who follow the prophetic advice share a good dream only with someone who loves them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'ijl, the calf made while people said they were waiting for Musa. Your line was wait for the one who's coming back. Today, a new story, told in full.
screen: `WAIT FOR THE ONE WHO'S COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: A boy wakes up and runs to tell his father about a dream. Almost everything we've heard about Ibrahim and Musa, the Qur'an tells in pieces, scattered across many surahs; you gather it up like shells on a beach. Yusuf's story is different. The Qur'an tells it start to finish, in order, in the surah named for him, and at the start it calls what follows the best of stories. For the next two weeks, we'll walk through it in order.
screen: `A BOY AND A DREAM.` → `ONE SURAH, START TO FINISH.` → `THE BEST OF STORIES.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf, verse four. Yusuf says: my father, I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon. I saw them bowing down to me. The Arabic for star, kawkab, can also mean a planet, and some older translations say eleven planets. Either way, the sky is kneeling to a boy. Commentators read the eleven stars as his eleven brothers, and the sun and the moon as his father and mother. It will take years, and a whole surah, to come true. Keep it in your pocket. Now Ya'qub, his father, a prophet himself. He doesn't laugh it off, and he doesn't tell the whole family at dinner. He says: my son, don't tell your dream to your brothers, or they'll plot against you. Satan is a clear enemy to people. He knows his sons, and the jealousy already simmering. So his first gift to Yusuf is discretion: some good things are safer kept close for a while. Then the hope: your Lord will choose you, and teach you the meaning of events, and complete His favor on you, as He completed it on your forefathers, Ibrahim and Ishaq. There's Ibrahim, from earlier on our path, standing in the family line. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave similar advice in a hadith: a good dream is from Allah, and you should tell it only to someone who loves you. Not every dream is for telling. And not everyone who hears it will be glad.

Hold it in your mind like a folded note in a pocket, and feel what it's like to keep it just for you: not out of fear, out of care, the way Ya'qub cared for his son. If you pray, you can give thanks for it quietly.

Your line: not every dream is for telling. Ya'qub's first gift to his son was a quiet one. Fifty-five days in.

56.title: The brothers' plan
56.hook: the brothers, jealous of their father's love, plot to be rid of Yusuf
56.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to guard against hasad, envy, and many say masha'Allah or pray for blessing on others when they see something good in someone else's life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: eleven stars, and a father who said keep it close. Your line was not every dream is for telling. Today closes the week.

Anyone with a sibling knows the math. Who got the bigger slice. Who got to sit in front. Whose drawing went on the fridge. It sounds petty written down, but it lives deep, and some families carry it for fifty years. Ya'qub has twelve sons. Two of them, Yusuf and his younger brother, are the sons of the wife he lost, and the older ten can see where their father's eyes rest. The Qur'an never says they heard about the dream. It doesn't need to. It lets us listen in on their conversation.
screen: `THE BIGGER SLICE.` → `TWELVE SONS, ONE FATHER.` → `WE LISTEN IN.`

segments.voice: The surah pauses first to tell us why we're listening: in Yusuf and his brothers there are signs for those who ask. This isn't only their family; it's everyone's. Then the brothers talk. Yusuf and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, and we are a strong group. Our father is plainly mistaken. Then someone says it: kill Yusuf, or throw him out into some far land, so your father's face will be yours alone. And after that, you can be righteous people. Listen to that last part. They're not only planning the wrong; they're planning the repentance. Jealousy is clever like that. It doesn't just feel. It schedules. Then one brother, the Qur'an doesn't name him, pulls them back from the worst: don't kill Yusuf. Throw him into the bottom of the well, and some travelers will pick him up. Still cruel. But one voice made it less cruel, and that matters later. The Arabic word for jealousy of this kind is hasad, wanting someone else's blessing taken from them. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, in a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim: don't envy one another, don't hate one another, don't turn your backs on one another; be servants of Allah, brothers. And that closes a week of hard rooms. Musa asking for an open chest. A gentle word to Pharaoh. The magicians. The sea. A golden calf. A boy's dream. And now brothers in a huddle, making plans.
screen: `SIGNS FOR THOSE WHO ASK.` · `DEARER TO OUR FATHER THAN WE.` · `AFTER THAT, WE'LL BE GOOD.` · `NOT KILL — THE WELL.` · then, large: `JEALOUSY MAKES PLANS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose life you've felt a pinch about lately, a friend's promotion, a sibling who seems to get the easy road, a stranger's vacation photos, and let the feeling come up without arguing with it. Name it softly, the way you'd name a cloud: that's jealousy; not I'm a terrible person, just there it is, and watch whether it's already making plans, even small ones. If you pray, you can ask for good for that person.
Hasad, envy: what drove the brothers to plot against Yusuf, and plan to be righteous people afterward.
Your line: jealousy makes plans. One voice in the huddle still made it less cruel. Day fifty-six, and a week complete.
